searchText: > If they use 51% coordination [to break out of the prisoner's dilema] they can just double spend, which is a *way* bigger problem (and way more profitable short-term). <@!301186049323958275> this is false equivalency because (a) the consequences to their wealth (ASICS and/or ETH holding) is not the same (b) There is plausible deniability here but not in double-spend; and they could set some threshold, say 10% of blocks, where they don't artificially require high tip and/or low basefee just to strengthen that deniability They would be fighting against their own supposed goals if they let 10% of their own blocks through at a lower price. no not really, that 10% is the price they agree on to strengthen their deniability vis a vis the community In order for this attack to be successful, they need to be censoring blocks of non-participants, similar to how one would in a double spend and it would be "obviously malicious". If they are unwilling to censor (because they want plausible deniability as you say), then the attack will not be profitable in any situation where users don't support the price increase and there isn't total control. The thing to keep in mind is that it is profitable to defect. That is what makes these systems so robust, because they are pseudoanonymous, and defection is profitable. So you tell other miners, "yeah, I'll join your cabal" and then you proceed to mine blocks under a different name that are below the cabal pricing. In fact, tricking other miners to join the cabal while you defect is a profitable strategy! So miners are incentivized to convince other miners to be in the cabal, but they all know that they all know that defecting is more profitable and undetectable, so no miner would rationally join a cabal. Five parties control 72% of Eth mining. Are you saying they can't come to a stable agreement with that 10% "ash in eyes" of blocks for deniability? Even without deniability, it wouldn't be profitable for them. Let's say 72% of hashing power agrees to mine blocks @10 nanoeth minimum tip. All of them are incentivized to mine blocks under another name at a price of 9 nanoeth, because they'll get much fuller blocks at an insignificant decrease in min tip. And all of the non-participants (those 28% remaining) will be mining full blocks below 10 nanoeth min-tip. So the 72% end up with less than half full blocks while defectors end up with full blocks. The defectors can go down to ~5.8 nanoeth min tip before being less profitable than the cabal participants. (the above assumes users aren't willing to pay double gas in exchange for mining 45 seconds faster, the actual formula is a bit complex once you include user price-time preference distribution). > All of them are incentivized to mine blocks under another name <@!301186049323958275> it'll be obvious though and the collusion is off. In real life though, collusions that may in game theoretical sense be unstable can be stable .. think of power/market sharing agreements between rival gangs The cabal would need extra-protocol pressures in place, and that is extremely hard to do with pseudoanonymous systems. In the case of gang territory, there is significant cost to warring, and defectors can be identified and punished. In cryptocurrency mining, it is very difficult to identify defectors, and even if you do it is very difficult to punish them. For example, lets say I join the cabal and state that I have 15% hashing power. I mine with the cabal but only with 13%. I can plausibly say that I lost some of my hashing power, when really I just am mining with 2% at an increased profit. Even if I mined with all 15% under a defection strategy, the rest of the cabal would need some mechanism of punishing me for defecting. Not punishing but they can detect your defection and yes the collusion is off or at least you are out of it...In real life a not-so-stable game can be stable as <@456226577798135808> said w.r.t. breaking out of prisoner dillema > it is very difficult to identify defectors <@!301186049323958275> I assumed the major pools don't change often so it's easy when the hashrate of one of them suddenly changes Even if you can detect defectors, you need a way to punish defectors. Remember, defectors make more money than the cabal as long as the cabal unless the cabal controls so much hashing power that the time delay of transactions mined by non-cabal participants is so high that users are unwilling to wait. what would you consider so much colluding hashing power? Side note: FWIW, miners *today* could exercise this exact same min-fee attack being described here. So this isn't really an argument against 1559 so much as it is an argument against gas going to miners at all. 🙂 > miners *today* could exercise this exact same min-fee attack <@!301186049323958275> the inefficient first-price auction is doing it for them 😁 A situation where a cabal *could* be stable would be if the cabal controlled 99% of hashing power and set the min-fee to 2 nanoeth (1.2 nanoeth profit per gas). The 1% of non-cabal participants could mine for 1.4 nanoeth (0.6 nanoeth profit per gas). The defector would always get 2x sized blocks, while participants would get *just* under half full blocks... but *ONLY* if ~1% of users are willing to wait 100 blocks longer to get mined in order to save 0.6 nanoeth per gas. If 1% of users are unwilling to wait 100 blocks longer to save 0.6 nanoeth on gas, then the cabal is stable. I would say there is a big chunk of users not willing to wait a few blocks given that a significant (majority?) of tx's today are (a) time-sensitive arbitrage and (b) transfers out of exchanges and they tend to set the fee very high (so they don't have to deal with customers complaining about delay), they don't give users the option to change it > Has https://gauntlet.network/ been considered for the formal analysis of the spec? They know very well the blockchain space, especially Ethereum. <@!278762485497069569> They gave us a quote in the $250k range, which would have been a decent start but it would not have answered all the questions we need answered. > I would say there is a big chunk of users not willing to wait a few blocks given that a significant (majority?) of tx's today are (a) time-sensitive arbitrage and (b) transfers out of exchanges and they tend to set the fee very high (so they don't have to deal with customers complaining about delay), they don't give users the option to change it I agree with that assertion. However, you only need a pretty small set of users willing to wait, and the number of users that need to wait is a function of how much hashing power is not participating in the cabal. So if your cabal is only 75%, I think you need ~25% of users willing to wait ~3 blocks in order to save `(cabal_premium - 0.8) / 2` gas price. This puts an upper bound on how much the cabal can extort, and as the cabal loses hashing power to defectors, the wait for users who support defectors (demand lower gas prices) decreases. As the cabal increases their premium, it increases the savings offered to users by profit-seeking defectors. There *are* some equilibriums in here where the cabal is stable, but the two of the inputs are "humans" (how long they are willing to wait and how much they demand to save in order to wait) which makes modeling difficult (output needs to either be a function or a multi-dimensional graph). My intuition says that the amount of power a cabal has in all situations is not significant enough to worry about, given the huge UX benefits of 1559. They are limited in how much they can jack up the gas price, and users can fight against cabals by just accepting a delay on their transaction (which makes defecting profitable). > and users can fight against cabals by just accepting a delay <@!301186049323958275> not sure if this is a reliable assumption (perfect information). we know from the status quo that the users would, collectively, save a lot of gas if they don't escalate and just chill a bit during spikes .. yet they do. > <@!574864862338088960> My plan was to push for 1559 to depend on 2718 after 2718 is final. I am hesitant to push for converting 1559 to depend on 2718 until then because depending on non-final EIPs can create a new roadblock in adoption. We should be aiming for that while constraining ourselves in terms of what's politically possible. 2718 before 1559 would be ideal, but we shouldn't slow down the 1559 release process because of 2718 politics. excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
> And from what I understand 1559 provides a much larger incentive for miners to collude to manipulate the base fee / block limit
I still have not seen a strong argument for this.  I am convinced that there are some weak incentives for collusion that can work under some very specific user behavior scenarios, but I think those scenarios are unlikely, and the amount of benefit from that collusion is pretty small.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: What I want to caution is pushing back 1559 solely due to fear of the unknown.  I don't think Ethereum is mature enough yet to set the bar of inclusion to "must have a formal proof to make a change".  I encourage people to try to think up and discuss viable attack scenarios and if someone comes up with one then I do think we should block 1559.  However, so far most of the arguments I have heard reduce to "this is a change, and change is scary" or "what if 51% of miners start censoring 49%" (which is an existing problem in Ethereum with much worse consequences).

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: That being said, this discussion has brought to light some limdted selfish collusion incentives under certain conditions, so I do think discussions like these are valuable.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: My *only* pushback is against fear of the unknown blocking protocol changes that have known benefits.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: I am operating under the assumption that 49% of miners can collude on *anything* and some significantly larger percentage can collude on anything that is not openly damaging the system.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: e.g., 90% can/will collude on gas price fixing, or block sizing.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: But, I *also* assume they will only do those things if it is profitable for them individually.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: That is, I assume they won't collude at personal cost to themselves in order to enrich someone else.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: I make no assumption that people won't *try* to price fix.  🙂

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: However, in traditional markets, successful price fixing usually requires a high barrier to entry for competition.  If the barrier to entry is low, then successful price fixing becomes quite difficult.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Hashing power has a very low barrier to entry, relatively speaking, so I'm not particularly worried about the traditional class of price fixing problem.
